title: The Bell is My Boss, Too
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: After hanging a "the bell is our boss" poster by his classroom clock, Stuart is surprised by how many students ask a natural follow-up question: if the bell means class starts the moment it rings, does that mean it also means class ends the moment it rings -- even mid-lesson? His answer is an unambiguous yes, and he explains why: he wants the ending bell to hold him personally accountable for pacing his lessons well, rather than letting himself run long as a habit. He frames this as an application of "Gentle Urgency," Strategy #3 in The Will to Learn, arguing that letting the bell govern both starts and ends keeps him disciplined about classroom time in both directions. He anticipates pushback from colleagues who might see this as making stricter teachers "look bad," but insists the real reason for the policy isn't optics or credibility with students, though it helps there too, but that it makes him a better, more disciplined teacher.
points: Stuart applies the "bell is our boss" framing symmetrically: if students are expected to self-govern into work the moment the bell starts class, fairness (and Gentle Urgency) requires it govern the end of class too.
He's explicit that letting the closing bell cut him off, even mid-lesson, is a deliberate constraint meant to keep his own pacing honest rather than letting lessons habitually run long.
He acknowledges but sets aside a plausible objection -- that this makes stricter colleagues "look bad" -- arguing that isn't his primary reason for the policy.

The piece frames a small classroom-management choice as identity-forming: "using the bell this way makes us better," tying a specific policy back to professional discipline rather than just fairness or likability.
quotes: None of you wants to hear an adult haranguing you each day to start class; that's unpleasant for you and it's unpleasant for me. That's a terrible way to start our time together. Because of that, we'll let the bell be our boss.
Yes — that is what that means. If I've not completed the lesson by the time the bell rings, that's my error and something I need to work on. You've got another class to get to in only five minutes.
I want to be the most gently efficient and competent teacher that I can be, and so I need that closing bell to mean that my class is over.

Otherwise, I'll get loosey-goosey with class endings and class middles and class beginnings. When the bell cuts me short, I want to be cut short, and I want to learn from the experience of having not finished the lesson.

And sure, telling my students that the bell is OUR boss, not just theirs — that does help with my Credibility by signaling that I'm fair. But that's not the most important reason to use the bell this way.
The most important reason is that using the bell this way makes us better.
